summary: First orientation for 5–7 year olds to the 'big picture' of space: Earth is one planet among several, the Sun together with the planets going around it is called the solar system, and space is the vast, mostly empty area far beyond Earth's sky. The goal at this age is orienting vocabulary and a rough mental map, not mechanism. The key conceptual move is decentring — helping children see Earth as one planet among others, not the whole of everything and not fundamentally different from the other planets — and distinguishing planets (which orbit the Sun and don't make their own light) from the Sun/stars. Because scale is unimaginable and unobservable at this age, teaching leans on zoom-out imagery, simple diagrams and playful orbiting role-play rather than numbers.
misconceptions: Earth is not a planet / Earth is separate from or bigger than 'the planets' (Earth is one planet among several)
The Sun is a planet, or planets and stars are the same kind of thing (planets orbit the Sun and don't make their own light)
Space 'starts' just above the rooftops / the sky and space are the same nearby thing (space is enormously far beyond the sky)
The solar system IS the whole universe / everything (it is just our Sun and its planets — a tiny part of a much bigger universe; formalised later)
The Sun goes around the Earth (leave cause aside, but avoid stories that entrench an Earth-centred picture)

activities.title: Zoom out from a familiar place into space
steps: Start on a familiar Earth scene — for example a park under a blue sky — then 'zoom out' in stages (on screen with a tap/button, or using a sequence of pictures/paper cards you reveal one at a time)
Watch the ground curve away until the child's whole world is just a blue-and-green ball floating in black
Zoom out again so that ball slides into place as one of several planets looping around a bright Sun, with the whole group labelled 'our solar system'

Name each part as you touch it: tap/point to Earth → 'Earth is a planet — one of several going around the Sun'; the Sun → 'the Sun gives light; the planets go around it'; the black between planets → 'space — the huge, mostly empty area far beyond our sky'
Open a lift-the-flap (or turn a card) answering 'where does space start?' by pointing up past the clouds, far above the sky (point toward the represented scene, not toward the real Sun)
activities.insight: Seeing their own Earth shrink to one ball among several is intended to help children feel that Earth is a planet like the others, not the whole world, and that space is enormously far beyond the everyday sky.

activities.title: Walk the orbit: become a planet going around the Sun
steps: Set up a central 'Sun' (a child, a lamp, or a marked spot) and have children walk in circles around it to act out 'the planets travel around the Sun'
Say the sentence as they move: 'the Sun stays in the middle while the planets go around it'
Point out that the Sun gives light while the planets do not make their own light — they are lit up by the Sun
Pause to 'find Earth' among the moving planets and confirm Earth is one of the ones going around
activities.insight: Acting out orbiting is intended to make 'the Sun and the planets that go around it' something children feel in their bodies, reinforcing the meaning of 'solar system' and that the Sun sits in the middle with planets circling it.

activities.title: Watch the planets orbit the Sun
steps: Press play on a simple Sun-with-orbiting-planets animation (or watch the walking-orbit game) and watch the planets circle the Sun
Tap/point to a planet to hear or say its name
Respond to a gentle 'find Earth' prompt and confirm Earth is one of the orbiting planets
activities.insight: Seeing 'going around the Sun' in motion is intended to make the orbit idea concrete and reinforce that Earth is one of several planets circling the Sun.

activities.title: Check: where things are and what counts as our solar system
steps: Match each word to its picture: planet / Sun / space

Sort pictures into 'on Earth / in the sky (e.g. clouds, birds, aeroplanes) / out in space (e.g. the Sun, Moon, planets, stars)', explaining that the Sun, Moon and stars can be seen in our sky but are really far away out in space
Pick 'which of these is our solar system?' from simple picture options showing the Sun with its planets
Answer and explain: 'Is Earth a planet, the same kind of thing as the other planets — or is Earth something different and special that isn't really a planet at all? Tell me which, and WHY'
activities.insight: Children can show they recognise Earth as a planet, name the solar system and place where space is — and the 'why' reveals whether they genuinely see Earth as one member of the solar system or are just reciting the word 'planet'. The 'something different and special' option is the misconception being probed, not a correct answer.

checkQuestion: Is the Earth a planet, the same kind of thing as the other planets in space — or is Earth something different and special that isn't really a planet at all? Tell me which, and WHY.
checkAnswer: Earth IS a planet — one of the planets that orbit the Sun. Our Sun together with the group of planets going round it is called the solar system. Earth feels special because we live on it, but it is the same KIND of thing as the other planets: a big ball travelling around the Sun.
